collection.description: A villager has been working too hard for too long.

ask.text:
(Name) has been working too hard for too long. Every day the same: up before dawn, work until dark, fall asleep, do it all again. This evening, sitting on (his/her) doorstep with aching shoulders, watching the children play tag on the beach and shriek with laughter, (he/she) sighs a long, long sigh.
"I wish I could be a child again," (he/she) says, out loud. "Just for a little while."
A passing breeze picks up the words. The elders always tell the children never to make wishes out loud on the evening breeze, because sometimes it listens. It's a warm one, coming off the beach, and it smells of sand and sugarcane and the long, golden summers of childhood. It swirls round (name), once, twice, lifting (his/her) hair. And (name) feels (his/her) feet slowly, gently, start to shrink. Should (name) enjoy being little, or wish to grow up again?

c1o1.text: (Name) spends the whole of the next day as a child. (He/She) plays tag on the beach and wins. (He/She) builds a sandcastle with a moat and a tower and three bridges. (He/She) climbs trees, eats fruit until (his/her) belly hurts, and falls asleep in the shade with sand on (his/her) face. And in the evening, as the sun sets, the same warm breeze comes back, and swirls round (him/her) again, and (he/she) is (himself/herself) once more, lying on the beach with aching shoulders and a very big grin. It was exactly what (he/she) needed.

c1o2.text: (Name) stays a child. The breeze doesn't come back. Not the next evening, or the one after that. And (name) doesn't seem to mind one bit. (He/She) plays tag every day, and builds sandcastles, and asks a thousand questions, and laughs, and laughs. (His/her) old friends are puzzled at first, then come to accept it. Everyone agrees that (name) seems happier than (he/she) has been in years. (He/She) still remembers all (his/her) old grown-up life. (He/She) just doesn't want it back yet.

c1.text: By the time the breeze has passed, (name) is sitting on the doorstep in a grown-up's wrap that's suddenly far too big, with small hands and small feet and a small, delighted face. (He/She) looks down at the beach, where the children are playing. Then (he/she) runs...

c2o1.text: The breeze stops. It turns round. And it seems to sigh, a little, as if (name) has disappointed it. Then it swirls round (him/her) once more, and (his/her) hands and feet grow back to their proper size, and (he/she) is standing on the path, (himself/herself) again, out of breath. But somehow, (he/she) feels better than before. More rested. As if (he/she) had had a whole long summer holiday in that one moment, and all the tiredness had blown away with the wind.

c2o2.text: The breeze has moved on. It's already away over the hills, and (name) can't catch it, and the more (he/she) runs, the smaller (he/she) gets, until (he/she) is tripping over (his/her) own wrap. By the time (he/she) stops, (he/she) is a little child, about six years old, standing alone on the path in the dusk, with a grown-up's memories and a very wobbly lip. (His/her) family come and find (him/her), and pick (him/her) up, and carry (him/her) home. The village helps (him/her) grow up all over again, and this time, everyone agrees, (he/she) is not to work so hard.

c2.text: (Name) looks down at (his/her) shrinking hands in horror. "No, no, no! Not like that! I didn't mean it! I take it back!" (He/She) jumps up, grown-up wrap trailing, and runs after the breeze down the path, shouting...
